Greenberg's potential flow model was originally developed to predict forces on helicopter blades undergoing harmonic motions in a pulsating stream.

The authors adapted Greenberg's model to handle the multi-harmonic oscillations in effective angle of attack and incoming flow velocity experienced by vertical-axis wind turbine blades, particularly at low tip-speed ratios.
The effective angle of attack and flow velocity variations were approximated using Fourier sine and cosine series, respectively, with N = 8 terms found to be sufficient.
Experiments were conducted on a scaled-down single-bladed H-type Darrieus wind turbine model in a water channel at a Reynolds number of 50,000.
The turbine blade had a NACA0018 profile with a chord of 6 cm, span of 15 cm, and chord-to-diameter ratio of 0.2.

The Greenberg model was able to well predict the radial forces at the start of the cycle and the maximum force coefficient during the upwind portion, even at low tip-speed ratios where dynamic stall occurred.

However, the model failed to capture the post-dynamic stall load response and the lower radial forces during the downwind portion of the cycle, which were attributed to flow separation and blade-wake interactions.

At higher tip-speed ratios (λ = 4.5), the Greenberg model was able to better predict the maximum radial load coefficient and its timing, but still underestimated the magnitude during the downwind portion.

The authors state that the adapted Greenberg model shows great potential for diagnosing regions of separated flow and quantifying the relative influences of dynamic stall and turbine kinematics on blade loading.
This work was supported by the Swiss national science foundation under grant number PYAPP2 173652.
The authors note that the Greenberg model's limitations stem from its basis in inviscid potential flow theory, which cannot capture viscous effects like flow separation and blade-wake interactions.
The authors propose that the method can be readily extended to model any airfoil undergoing arbitrary combinations of pitching, surging, and heaving motions.
The Fourier series approximations used to represent the turbine blade kinematics were found to accurately fit the true variations, with negligible differences for tip-speed ratios λ ≥ 1.2.
The experimental setup included a recirculating water channel with a test section of 0.6m x 0.6m x 3m and a maximum flow velocity of 1 m/s.
The static stall angle for the NACA0018 airfoil at the experimental Reynolds number of 50,000 was 13.1 degrees.
